transcript.text: Section 3. You will hear two students called Ruth and Edward discussing their assignment
about a conservation issue involving elephants in Kenya. First, you have some time to look
at questions 21 to 24. Now, listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 24.
Ruth: Right, Edward. I've got some notes here for our conservation assignment. I had a look at the
research you mentioned in Kenya. I hadn't realized that farmers were having so many problems with
elephants eating their crops there. Edward: Yes, the trouble is when elephants get into farmers' fields and
destroy their crops, that has all sorts of other results. Ruth: I don't suppose the farmers can just get
up and go somewhere else. Edward: No, but it's a real problem because farmers are shooting the elephants
to keep their crops safe. And then the other elephants are affected and become very hostile to humans.
But you can see for the farmers it's not homes and families that have been threatened.
Ruth: And it's understandable that farmers don't feel like supporting elephant conservation
if their own livelihood is being destroyed. You feel you have the right to defend your property. Edward: Exactly.
So I thought for our assignment we can start with the problem then introduce the
solutions they've been experimenting with. Ruth: So now we get on to the bees. I never thought elephants
would be afraid of bees. But I suppose even if you're as big as an elephant a bee sting can still hurt.
Edward: Well I think it depends. Bees can't sting through the thick skin on an adult elephant's body
but they target the sensitive areas like near the eyes. Ruth: Oh that must really hurt and I heard they
get right inside the elephant's trunk and sting there. Edward: Yes and then there are the baby elephants,
the calves which have thinner skin so they can be really badly affected especially if they get
attacked by a whole swarm of bees. Ruth: So elephants with babies may be threatened by bees even if they
don't get stung themselves.
Before you hear the rest of the discussion you have some time to read questions 25 to 30.
Now listen and answer questions 25 to 30.
Edward: Okay, so next we can go on to describe the experiments based on this fear that elephants have
of bees. So there was one way they hung containers full of bees in trees near the farms and they
listened in trees without containers and they found the elephants trampled down the trees that
didn't have any containers and stayed well away from the ones with the bees in.
Ruth: Okay, so did you read the articles about the experiment where it was done with the audio recording of bees instead
of real bees? Edward: No. Ruth: Well, they've got a recording of a swarm of angry bees and they played it to
herds of elephants out in the wild and they all stopped what they were doing immediately and stood
erect with their heads up and their ears extended. Edward: They must have been really aware there was danger
somewhere. Ruth: But not the sort of danger that they can face up to and charge, so they dashed off in the
opposite direction. They kept turning their heads around.
Edward: Presumably looking for the swarm of bees which wasn't there. Ruth: Yes, and researchers tested 18 different herds of the elephants and all but
one responded in the same way. Edward: Maybe that herd just didn't hear it properly.
It seems a very small exception to the main finding. Ruth: I think researchers actually concluded that this particular herd lacked
any experience of bees. They'd never encountered any so they weren't afraid of the recording. Edward: Right.
Oh so that was the reason. Ruth: Exactly. But what surprised the researchers was, from the
17 herds that did take action when they heard the recording, they found almost 50% of the herds
did this very quickly within 10 seconds of hearing the recording. Edward: Oh that's interesting.
Ruth: Right. So playing the recordings of bees could be a good deterrent to elephants but it's not all
that straightforward actually. Edward: Yes, you've got to have the electricity to run the machinery.
Ruth: No, that's okay. It can run on batteries, but the whole thing's quite difficult for electrical outlet
which might be easy and then someone's got to set it all out and make sure it's working.
That's not difficult but it's really a job.
Edward: They're trying other methods as well like electric fences to keep the elephants away from the crops. They haven't had much success but when they
hang cowbells on the fences that seemed to scare them off.
Ruth: Yes, I've read they tried chili peppers as a deterrent too but that didn't scare the elephants at all. Edward: Right, so I think we've got plenty
of information.
That is the end of section 3. You now have half a minute to check your answers.
